{{ElectionsME}}

The '''2026 Maine gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. Incumbent [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] governor [[Janet Mills]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. Although Maine has adopted [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]], it is only used for primary and federal general elections. Therefore, the primary was conducted with ranked-choice voting, and the general election will be conducted with the traditional [[Plurality voting|plurality voting]] system. [[Primary elections]] were held on June 9, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2025-05-23 |website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}}</ref>

Democrat [[Hannah Pingree]] and Republican [[Robert B. Charles|Bobby Charles]] won their respective primaries, and will be joined on the ballot by independent [[Rick Bennett (Maine politician)|Rick Bennett]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=Hannah Pingree wins ranked-choice runoff in Democratic primary for governor |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/19/hannah-pingree-wins-ranked-choice-runoff-in-democratic-primary-for-governor/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Background ==
Incumbent Democratic governor [[Janet Mills]] was re-elected with 55.69% of the vote in [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]] over Republican former governor [[Paul LePage]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2022-11-09 |title=Maine Gov. Janet Mills wins second term, defeating former GOP Gov. Paul LePage |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/11/09/1134198072/maine-election-results-governor-paul-lepage-janet-mills |access-date=2026-01-20 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref> She is term-limited and not eligible to run again.

A sparsely populated state in [[New England]], Maine is one of the most [[Rural areas in the United States|rural]] states in the nation and is considered to be moderately [[Red states and blue states|blue]]. Both houses of the [[Maine Legislature]] were controlled by the Maine Democratic Party in the prior session. A Republican has not received 50% or more of the vote in a gubernatorial election since [[1962 Maine gubernatorial election|1962]], when incumbent Republican [[John H. Reed]] received 50.08% of the vote.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Maine Election Returns |url=https://www.maine.gov/legis/lawlib/lldl/elections/electionshome.html |access-date=2026-01-20 |website=www.maine.gov}}</ref>

==Democratic primary==
[[Shenna Bellows]], [[Troy Jackson]], and [[Hannah Pingree]] announced an "alliance" on May 22, 2026, in which they would rank each other ahead of their opponents [[Angus King III]] and [[Nirav D. Shah|Nirav Shah]]; Shah was leading in most public polls.<ref name="PingreeJacksonBellowsAlliance">{{Cite web |last=Brodey |first=Sam |date=May 28, 2026 |title=It has famous names, wildcards, and a COVID doctor: How Maine's governor race became the primary to watch - The Boston Globe |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/05/28/nation/maine-janet-mills-governor-race-graham-platner/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=BostonGlobe.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Shah received the most first-preference votes, with 26.8%, followed by Pingree with 23.3%, Jackson with 21.0%, Bellows with 20.7%, and King with 8.2%. As a result of finishing last, King was eliminated and his voters' second preferences were redistributed to the remaining four candidates. Pingree was ultimately nominated after four rounds of ranked-choice tabulation, defeating Shah in the final round by a 56%–44% margin.<ref name=":7" />

Following his loss in the gubernatorial primary, [[Troy Jackson]] became the Democratic nominee in the [[2026 United States Senate election in Maine|2026 United States Senate election]] after former nominee [[Graham Platner]] withdrew from the race.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Emma |date=2026-07-25 |title=Troy Jackson officially clinches Maine Democratic U.S. Senate nomination • Maine Morning Star |url=https://mainemorningstar.com/2026/07/25/troy-jackson-officially-clinches-maine-democratic-u-s-senate-nomination/ |access-date=2026-09-23 |website=Maine Morning Star |language=en-US}}</ref>

The Maine gubernatorial election uses [[instant-runoff voting]] as its algorithm: in each round, the candidate with the fewest [[first-preference vote]]s among the remaining candidates is eliminated, and each ballot which was formerly voting for that candidate is transferred to its new first preference.  This necessarily results in a number of rounds equal to 1 less than the number of candidates.

==Republican primary==
All Republican candidates said that they opposed ranked choice voting. [[Robert B. Charles|Robert Charles]] was particularly critical of ranked choice voting and encouraged Republican primary voters to rank him across the ballot and not rank other candidates. Charles criticized what he called "back room deals" among other candidates to encourage their supporters to rank another candidate second, claiming other candidates could not be trusted to work to repeal ranked choice voting while encouraging its use.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2026-05-15 |title=Looking to topple Bobby Charles, Maine's GOP primary candidates are turning to an unlikely tool |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-15/looking-to-topple-bobby-charles-maines-gop-primary-candidates-are-turning-to-an-unlikely-tool|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Miller |first=Kevin |date=2026-05-08 |title=Some, but not all, GOP gubernatorial candidates are embracing ranked-choice voting |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-08/some-but-not-all-gop-gubernatorial-candidates-are-embracing-ranked-choice-voting|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The candidates who endorsed a second choice were Robert Wessels, who endorsed [[Jonathan S. Bush|Jonathan Bush]] as his second choice, Ben Midgley, who endorsed David Jones as his second choice, and David Jones, who endorsed Midgley as his second choice.

Charles would win 37.7% of the vote, with Midgley and Bush finishing with 20.1% and 19.8% respectively, and every other candidate some distance behind them. State senator [[James D. Libby|James Libby]], who had suspended his campaign in April but did not formally withdrawn from the race, finished in last.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2026-06-10 |title=What to watch for as Maine races head to ranked-choice runoffs |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/10/what-to-watch-for-as-maine-races-head-to-ranked-choice-runoffs/ |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref> After seven rounds of ranked-choice voting tabulation, Charles was declared the winner.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=Bobby Charles holds lead to win Republican primary for governor after RCV runoff |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/19/bobby-charles-holds-lead-to-win-republican-primary-for-governor-after-rcv-runoff/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Convention vote ===
On April 25, 2026, the Maine Republican Party announced the results of a straw poll by delegates to the Maine Republican Convention. Robert Charles was declared the winner.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newscentermaine.com/article/news/politics/maine-politics/maine-republican-convention-governor-gubernatorial-candidates-election/97-de11da9a-f97e-4251-be85-b4ee45721572|work=WCSH-TV|last=Hirschkorn|first=Phil|date=April 25, 2026|title=Blaine House hopefuls make their case to delegates on second day of Maine Republican convention}}</ref> Unlike the primary, the straw poll was conducted without ranked-choice voting, and was non-binding.
